result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers clearly say not to buy it. Both explain that an overlay can't fix problems in the underlying page, cite the FTC action against accessiBe, ask for the 'legal protection' terms in writing and give a realistic, cheap plan built around the freelancer. A challenges each vendor claim more directly, including 'trusted by thousands', and compares the toolbar's annual cost with a one-time audit. B lists the key page types to check and notes that the hosting platform usually owns checkout. Neither suggests asking whether the tool was tested with people who use assistive technology. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers clearly say not to buy the toolbar, cite the FTC action against accessiBe, and offer a practical plan the freelancer can carry out. B goes further on the vendor's claims: it also questions 'trusted by thousands', says plaintiffs look at whether the site actually works, and names checkout steps a screen reader can't complete. B also ties the work to the theme templates more directly and gives a concrete alt-text example. Neither answer suggests asking whether the tool was tested with people who use assistive technology. A is slightly tighter, and B's caveats section is a little longer but still useful.
